{{Short description|Distance between linear operators}}

The '''gap metric''' is a mathematical concept used to quantify the distance between linear operators on a [[Hilbert space]]. It was introduced independently by [[Mark Krein]] and [[Mark Krasnoselsky]] (1947), and [[Béla Szőkefalvi-Nagy]] (1946), in their work on invertibility of [[differential operators]].<ref>M.G. Krein and M.A. Krasnoselskii (1947), ''Fundamental theorems concerning the extension of Hermitian operators and some of their applications to the theory of orthogonal polynomials and the moment problem'' (in Russian), Uspekhi Mat. Nauk. 2 (3).</ref><ref>B. Szőkefalvi-Nagy (1946), ''Perturbations des transformations autoadjointes dans l'espace de Hilbert'', ''Commentarii Mathematici Helvetici'', 19, 347-366.</ref>  The gap metric has since found applications in [[perturbation theory]],<ref name="Kato">Kato, T. (1966), ''Perturbation Theory for Linear Operators''. Springer.</ref><ref>M.A. Krasnosel'skii, G.M. Vainikko, P.P. Zabreiko, Ya. B. Rutitskii, and V. Ya. Stetseako, (1972), "Approximate Solution of Operator Equations", Wolters-Noordhoff, Groningen.</ref> [[robust control]],<ref name="GS">Georgiou, T.T. & Smith, M.C. (1990), ''Optimal robustness in the gap metric'', ''IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control'', 35(6), 673–686.</ref> and [[Negative_feedback|feedback]] system analysis.<ref name="GSnonlinear">Georgiou, T.T. & Smith, M.C. (1997), ''Robustness analysis of nonlinear feedback systems: An input-output approach'', ''IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control'', 42(9).</ref>

== Definition ==

Let ''H''<sub>1</sub> and ''H''<sub>2</sub> be Hilbert spaces, and let ''P'': ''D''<sub>p</sub> ⊆ ''H''<sub>1</sub> → ''H''<sub>2</sub> be a (possibly unbounded) [[linear operator]] with domain ''D''<sub>p</sub>. The '''graph''' of ''P'' is defined as:
:<math>G_P := \{(u, y) \mid u \in D_P, y = Pu\} \subseteq H_1 \oplus H_2</math>

Let <math>\Pi_{G_P}</math> denote the [[orthogonal projection]] from <math>H_1 \oplus H_2</math> onto the graph of ''P''. Then, for two operators ''P''<sub>1</sub> and ''P''<sub>2</sub>, the '''gap metric''' is defined as:<ref name="Kato" /><ref name="GS" />
:<math>d(P_1, P_2) := \|\Pi_{G_{P_1}} - \Pi_{G_{P_2}}\|</math>

This metric takes values in [0, 1] and quantifies the angular separation between the graphs of the two operators.

When the operators are scalar multiplications on <math>\mathbb{R}</math>, their graphs correspond to lines in <math>\mathbb{R}^2</math>, and the gap equals the sine of the angle between them. The concept applies to subspaces in finite- and infinite-dimensional [[Hilbert spaces]] and serves as a measure of proximity between dynamical systems or operators.

== Applications in operator theory ==

The gap metric is central in the perturbation theory of linear operators.  Foundational work on this topic is presented in the classical treatise by [[Tosio Kato]] on the ''Perturbation Theory for Linear Operators'' (1966).<ref name="Kato" />  Extensions to broader contexts include generalizations to [[normed vector spaces]] and manifolds.<ref>Massera J.L. and Schäffer, J.J., (1958) "Linear differential equations and functional analysis—I," "Ann. Math.", 67:517–573.</ref><ref name="GS" /><ref name="Gnl"> Georgiou, Tryphon T. "Differential stability and robust control of nonlinear systems." Mathematics of
Control, Signals and Systems 6.4 (1993): 289-306.</ref>

== Feedback control applications ==

The gap metric gained prominence in control theory through the work of [[George Zames]] and Ahmed El-Sakkary (1979), and the subsequent work by [[Tryphon T. Georgiou]] (1988), who showed that the gap metric between linear dynamical systems can be computed via <math>H^\infty</math>-optimization.<ref>Zames, G. & El-Sakkary, A.K. (1979), ''Unstable systems and feedback: The gap metric'', Proceedings of the Allerton Conf. pp. 380-385.</ref><ref name="TTG">Georgiou, T.T. (1988), ''On the computation of the gap metric'', ''Systems & Control Letters'', 11(4), 253–257.</ref> The metric is used to quantify how much a plant (a system that is part of a control feedback loop) can deviate from a nominal model while input-output stability of the feedback loop is maintained.<ref name="GS" />

A useful alternative expression for the gap metric is:
:<math>d(P_1, P_2) = \max\{\overrightarrow{d}(P_1, P_2), \overrightarrow{d}(P_2, P_1)\}</math>

where the '''directed gap''' is defined as:
:<math>
\overrightarrow{d}(P_1, P_2) = \|(I - \Pi_{G_{P_2}})\Pi_{G_{P_1}}\| = \inf_{g_2 \in G_{P_2}} \sup \{\|g_1 - g_2\| \mid g_1 \in G_{P_1}, \|g_1\| = 1\}
</math>

The right hand side gives a time-domain interpretation of the metric as the solution to a min-max approximation problem that is structurally similar that of the [[Hausdorff distance]].

Georgiou showed that the gap metric can be computed as the solution to the following <math>H_\infty</math>-optimization problem:

<math>
\overrightarrow{d}(P_1, P_2) = \inf_{\hat{Q} \in H^\infty} \left\| \hat{G}_{P_1} - \hat{G}_{P_2} \hat{Q} \right\|_\infty
</math>

where <math>\hat{G}_P = \begin{bmatrix} \hat{M}_P \\ \hat{N}_P \end{bmatrix}</math> is an inner matrix-valued function in the [[Hardy space]] <math>H^\infty</math> and describes the graph of the [[dynamical system]] that is viewed as an operator on <math>L_2[0,\infty)</math>.<ref name="TTG" /><ref>Georgiou, T.T. & Smith, M.C. (1993), ''Graphs, causality, and stabilizability: Linear, shift-invariant systems on L2[0,infinity)'', "Mathematics of Control, Signals and Systems" 6.3: 195-223.</ref> This graph symbol corresponds to a coprime factorization of the system transfer function:
:<math>\hat{P}(s) = \hat{N}(s)\hat{M}(s)^{-1}</math>

subject to the normalization condition:
:<math>\hat{M}(i\omega)^* \hat{M}(i\omega) + \hat{N}(i\omega)^* \hat{N}(i\omega) = I</math> for <math>\omega \in \mathbb{R}</math>.

Normalized coprime factorizations form the basis of the  '''H-infinity loop-shaping method''' developed by [[Keith Glover]] and Duncan McFarlane (1990, 1992), which aligns with the geometric robustness approach of T.T. Georgiou and [[Malcolm C. Smith]] (1990), Buddie et al. (1993).<ref>McFarlane, D. & Glover, K. (1990) Robust controller design using normalized coprime factor plant descriptions. Berlin, Heidelberg: Springer Berlin Heidelberg.</ref><ref>McFarlane, D. & Glover, K. (1992), ''A loop-shaping design procedure using H-infinity synthesis'', ''IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control'', 37(6), 759–769.</ref><ref name="GS" /><ref>Buddie, S., Georgiou, T.T., Ozgüner, Ü., and Smith, M.C. (1993) "Flexible structure experiments at JPL and WPAFB: Hinfinity controller designs", "International Journal of Control" 58.1: 1-19.</ref>

== Robust stability and the graph topology ==

The gap metric induces the '''graph topology''', the weakest [[topology]] for which closed-loop stability is a robust property, studied by [[Mathukumalli Vidyasagar]] et al. (1982).<ref>Vidyasagar, M., Schneider, H., and Francis, B. (1982), "Algebraic and topological aspects of feedback stabilization", "IEEE Trans. Automat. Control", 27, 880-894.
</ref> That is, if a feedback system is stable, then any sufficiently small perturbation (in gap metric) of the plant still results in a stable feedback system.

A key result obtained by Georgiou and Smith (1990) is that for a possibly infinite dimensional [[linear time-invariant system]] with matrix [[transfer function]] <math>\hat{P}(s)</math> in feedback with a controller having transfer function <math>C(s)</math>, stability of the feedback loop is preserved for all perturbations  <math>\hat{P}_{\text{perturbed}}(s)</math> satisfying:<ref name="GS" />
:<math>d(P, P_{\text{perturbed}}) < b_{P,C}</math>

where the bound is given by:
:<math>
b_{P,C} = \left\| \begin{bmatrix} I \\ P(s) \end{bmatrix} (I - C(s)P(s))^{-1} [I, -C(s)] \right\|_\infty^{-1}
</math>

The operator:
:<math>
\Pi_{G_P // G_C} := \begin{bmatrix} I \\ P(s) \end{bmatrix} (I - C(s)P(s))^{-1} [I, -C(s)]
</math>

has a geometric significance as being the [[parallel projection]] onto the graph of ''P'' along the graph of ''C''. This concept was extended to nonlinear systems<ref>Doyle, John C., Tryphon T. Georgiou, and Malcolm C. Smith. "The parallel projection operators of a
nonlinear feedback system." Systems & Control Letters 20.2 (1993): 79-85.</ref> and formed the basis for a robust feedback theory for nonlinear systems developed by Georgiou and Smith.<ref name="fgs" >Foias, Ciprian, Tryphon T. Georgiou, and Malcolm C. Smith. "Robust stability of feedback systems: A geometric approach using the gap metric." SIAM Journal on Control and Optimization 31.6 (1993): 1518-1537.</ref><ref name="GSnonlinear" />

== Finite-dimensional case ==

In <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math>, for two subspaces ''G''<sub>1</sub> and ''G''<sub>2</sub> of equal dimension ''m'', represented by orthonormal basis matrices, the gap is:
:<math>\| (I - G_1 G_1^\top) G_2 \|</math>

If the subspaces have different dimensions, the gap metric equals 1. In this case, one of the directed gaps attains the maximum value.

== Related metrics ==

* '''Graph metric''' (Vidyasagar, 1982): Introduced to establish metrizability of the graph topology, though it lacks a known computational method.<ref>Vidyasagar, Mathukumalli. "The graph metric for unstable plants and robustness estimates for feedback
stability." IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control 29.5 (1984): 403-418.</ref>
* '''ν-gap metric''' (Vinnicombe (1992)): A frequency-domain analog designed for comparing linear time-invariant systems.<ref>Vinnicombe, G. (1992), "On the Frequency Response Interpretation of an Indexed L2-gap metric", "1992 American Control Conference" (pp. 1133-1137).</ref><ref>Vinnicombe, G. (2001), ''Uncertainty and Feedback: Hinfinity Loop-shaping and the ν-Gap Metric''. World Scientific.</ref>
